questiontext.text:
Match the microsporangium components in List I with their corresponding structural or functional descriptions in List II.

List I (Structure)List II (Function / Feature)
(a) Epidermis(i) Nourishes developing pollen grains
(b) Endothecium(ii) Undergoes meiosis to form microspore tetrads
(c) Tapetum(iii) Outermost single protective wall layer
(d) Sporogenous tissue(iv) Outer wall layer aiding in anther dehiscence

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A typical microsporangium in an angiosperm anther consists of four concentric wall layers surrounding a central mass of homogeneous sporogenous cells.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- The epidermis is the outermost single protective wall layer of the microsporangium.
- The endothecium lies beneath the epidermis and, along with the outer layers, performs protection and aids in the dehiscence of the anther to release pollen.
- The tapetum is the innermost wall layer with dense cytoplasm and often multiple nuclei; it nourishes the developing pollen grains.
- The sporogenous tissue occupies the centre of each young microsporangium and its cells undergo meiotic divisions to form microspore tetrads.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Epidermis — Outermost single protective wall layer; Endothecium — Outer wall layer aiding in anther dehiscence; Tapetum — Nourishes developing pollen grains; Sporogenous tissue — Undergoes meiosis to form microspore tetrads (a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q02 - Pollen grain wall and cellular parts

questiontext.text:
Match the pollen grain structures in List I with their characteristic features in List II.

List I (Part)List II (Characteristic)
(a) Exine(i) Thin, continuous layer made of cellulose and pectin
(b) Intine(ii) Prominent apertures where sporopollenin is absent
(c) Germ pores(iii) Hard outer layer composed of sporopollenin
(d) Vegetative cell(iv) Larger cell with abundant food reserve and irregular nucleus

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The pollen grain represents the male gametophyte and is enclosed by a two-layered wall (exine and intine) containing a vegetative cell and a generative cell at maturity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- The exine is the hard outer layer made up of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known.
- The intine is the thin, continuous inner wall made up of cellulose and pectin.
- Germ pores are prominent apertures in the exine where sporopollenin is absent, allowing the pollen tube to emerge.
- The vegetative cell is the larger cell of the mature pollen grain, containing abundant food reserves and a large, irregularly shaped nucleus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Exine — Hard outer layer composed of sporopollenin; Intine — Thin, continuous layer made of cellulose and pectin; Germ pores — Prominent apertures where sporopollenin is absent; Vegetative cell — Larger cell with abundant food reserve and irregular nucleus (a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q03 - Gynoecium types and ovule number examples

questiontext.text:
Match the gynoecium and ovule characteristics in List I with their corresponding plant examples in List II.

List I (Feature)List II (Examples)
(a) Multicarpellary, syncarpous pistil(i) Michelia
(b) Multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium(ii) Wheat, paddy, mango
(c) Single ovule in an ovary(iii) Papaver
(d) Many ovules in an ovary(iv) Papaya, water melon, orchids

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Multicarpellary gynoecia are classified as syncarpous (carpels fused) or apocarpous (carpels free), and ovaries vary in the number of ovules they contain.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- A multicarpellary, syncarpous pistil (fused carpels) is seen in Papaver.
- A multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium (free carpels) is seen in Michelia.
- A single ovule in an ovary is characteristic of wheat, paddy, and mango.
- Many ovules in an ovary are found in papaya, water melon, and orchids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Multicarpellary, syncarpous pistil — Papaver; Multicarpellary, apocarpous gynoecium — Michelia; Single ovule in an ovary — Wheat, paddy, mango; Many ovules in an ovary — Papaya, water melon, orchids (a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q04 - Types of pollination and genetic outcomes

questiontext.text:
Match the types of pollination in List I with their defining features in List II.

List I (Pollination Type)List II (Defining Feature)
(a) Autogamy(i) Transfer of pollen to another flower of the same plant
(b) Geitonogamy(ii) Brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma
(c) Xenogamy(iii) Assured seed-set in unopened flowers without pollinators
(d) Cleistogamy(iv) Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pollination is categorised into autogamy, geitonogamy, and xenogamy based on the source of pollen, while cleistogamy represents a specialised self-pollinating floral condition.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Autogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower.
- Geitonogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower of the same plant (functionally cross-pollination, but genetically similar to autogamy).
- Xenogamy is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a different plant, which is the only type bringing genetically different pollen to the stigma.
- Cleistogamy occurs in flowers that do not open at all, producing assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Autogamy — Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower; Geitonogamy — Transfer of pollen to another flower of the same plant; Xenogamy — Brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma; Cleistogamy — Assured seed-set in unopened flowers without pollinators (a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q05 - Agents of pollination and plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match the modes of pollination in List I with the appropriate plant examples in List II.

List I (Mode of Pollination)List II (Plant Examples)
(a) Wind pollination(i) Zostera (marine sea-grass)
(b) Surface water pollination(ii) Water hyacinth and water lily
(c) Submerged water pollination(iii) Grasses and corn cob
(d) Insect or wind pollination in aquatic plants(iv) Vallisneria

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Abiotic pollination occurs via wind or water, whereas many aquatic plants whose flowers emerge above water still rely on insects or wind rather than water.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Wind pollination is common in grasses and is classically seen in the corn cob, where tassels (stigma and style) wave in the wind.
- Surface water pollination occurs in Vallisneria, where the female flower reaches the water surface by a long stalk and pollen grains float passively on the surface.
- Submerged water pollination occurs in marine sea-grasses such as Zostera, where female flowers remain submerged and ribbon-like pollen grains are released inside water.
- Insect or wind pollination in aquatic plants occurs in water hyacinth and water lily, whose flowers emerge above the water level.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Wind pollination — Grasses and corn cob; Surface water pollination — Vallisneria; Submerged water pollination — Zostera; Insect or wind pollination in aquatic plants — Water hyacinth and water lily (a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii).

questiontext.text:
Match the outbreeding devices in List I with how they discourage self-pollination in List II.

List I (Outbreeding Device)List II (Mechanism)
(a) Non-synchronised pollen release and stigma receptivity(i) Prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy
(b) Different spatial positions of anther and stigma(ii) Prevents pollen from contacting stigma of the same flower
(c) Self-incompatibility(iii) Genetic mechanism inhibiting self-pollen germination or tube growth
(d) Dioecy (e.g., papaya)(iv) Prevents autogamy by temporal separation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Flowering plants employ temporal, spatial, genetic, and floral-distribution strategies as outbreeding devices to prevent inbreeding depression.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Non-synchronised pollen release and stigma receptivity prevents autogamy by separating male and female readiness in time (temporal separation).
- Different spatial positions of anther and stigma ensure that pollen cannot come into contact with the stigma of the same flower.
- Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen from fertilising ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
- Dioecy (male and female flowers on separate plants, as in papaya) prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Non-synchronised pollen release and stigma receptivity — Prevents autogamy by temporal separation; Different spatial positions of anther and stigma — Prevents pollen from contacting stigma of the same flower; Self-incompatibility — Genetic mechanism inhibiting self-pollen germination or tube growth; Dioecy — Prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy (a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q07 - Ploidy levels of reproductive cells and nuclei

questiontext.text:
Match the reproductive structures or nuclei in List I with their correct ploidy and cellular status in List II.

List I (Structure / Nucleus)List II (Ploidy / Status)
(a) Pollen mother cell(i) Triploid (\(3n\))
(b) Synergid(ii) Two haploid (\(n + n\)) nuclei in central cell
(c) Primary endosperm nucleus(iii) Diploid (\(2n\))
(d) Polar nuclei (before fusion)(iv) Single haploid (\(n\)) cell of egg apparatus

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sporophytic tissues and mother cells prior to meiosis are diploid (\(2n\)), gametophytic cells formed from spores are haploid (\(n\)), and the product of triple fusion is triploid (\(3n\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- A pollen mother cell is a sporogenous cell that undergoes meiosis to form microspores; hence, it is diploid (\(2n\)).
- A synergid is one of the cells of the egg apparatus in the haploid female gametophyte; hence, it is a single haploid (\(n\)) cell.
- The primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) is formed by triple fusion of one haploid male gamete (\(n\)) with two haploid polar nuclei (\(n + n\)), making it triploid (\(3n\)).
- The polar nuclei (prior to triple fusion) consist of two haploid (\(n + n\)) nuclei situated in the large central cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Pollen mother cell — Diploid (\(2n\)); Synergid — Single haploid (\(n\)) cell of egg apparatus; Primary endosperm nucleus — Triploid (\(3n\)); Polar nuclei — Two haploid (\(n + n\)) nuclei in central cell (a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q08 - Seed and fruit classifications with examples

questiontext.text:
Match the seed and fruit categories in List I with their correct examples in List II.

List I (Category)List II (Examples)
(a) Non-albuminous seed(i) Black pepper and beet
(b) Albuminous seed(ii) Apple and strawberry
(c) Seed with persistent perisperm(iii) Pea and groundnut
(d) False fruit(iv) Wheat, maize, and castor

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Seeds are classified based on whether endosperm or nucellus persists at maturity, and fruits are classified as true or false based on whether floral parts other than the ovary contribute to fruit formation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Non-albuminous (ex-albuminous) seeds have no residual endosperm as it is completely consumed during embryo development, as seen in pea and groundnut.
- Albuminous seeds retain a part of the endosperm, as seen in wheat, maize, barley, and castor.
- Seeds with persistent perisperm retain remnants of the nucellus, as seen in black pepper and beet.
- False fruits are formed when the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation alongside the ovary, as seen in apple, strawberry, and cashew.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Non-albuminous seed — Pea and groundnut; Albuminous seed — Wheat, maize, and castor; Seed with persistent perisperm — Black pepper and beet; False fruit — Apple and strawberry (a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_SEXUALREPRODUCTIONINFLOWERINGPLANTS_MATCH_Q09 - Special reproductive phenomena and plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match the special reproductive phenomena or seed records in List I with their corresponding descriptions or examples in List II.

List I (Phenomenon / Record)List II (Example / Description)
(a) Parthenocarpy(i) Lupinus arcticus
(b) Apomixis(ii) Nucellar embryos in Citrus and Mango
(c) Polyembryony(iii) Seedless fruit formed without fertilisation (e.g., banana)
(d) 10,000-year seed dormancy(iv) Seed formation without fertilisation (e.g., Asteraceae and grasses)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain angiosperms exhibit specialised deviations from typical sexual reproduction, including fruit or seed development without fertilisation, multiple embryos per seed, and extreme seed longevity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
- Parthenocarpy is the development of seedless fruits without fertilisation, as seen in banana.
- Apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction mimicking sexual reproduction in which seeds are produced without fertilisation, as seen in some species of Asteraceae and grasses.
- Polyembryony is the occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed, commonly arising when nucellar cells divide and protrude into the embryo sac in Citrus and Mango varieties.
- 10,000-year seed dormancy is the oldest recorded viable seed, belonging to the arctic lupine Lupinus arcticus excavated from Arctic Tundra.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Parthenocarpy — Seedless fruit formed without fertilisation; Apomixis — Seed formation without fertilisation; Polyembryony — Nucellar embryos in Citrus and Mango; 10,000-year seed dormancy — Lupinus arcticus (a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i).
